extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy (Schopenhauer / metaphysics / ethics)
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from Schopenhauer's The World as Will and Representation discussing the nature of the will, character, repentance, deliberation, and suffering; it develops normative and explanatory claims about human action and ethical psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repentance as corrected knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Repentance never proceeds from a change of the will (which is impossible), but from a change of knowledge; the discovery through fuller knowledge that an action did not conform to one's will is repentance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repentance manifests by making amends for the past where possible. Anguish of conscience for past deeds is not repentance (it is pain at the knowledge of oneself as will). People may feign hasty errors to deceive themselves; true repentance arises when motives are correctly understood and the relation of an act to its special intention is corrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between human and brute choice (deliberation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human choice is possible because man, unlike brutes, possesses abstract ideas and can deliberate: several motives can be held 'in abstracto' and weighed, producing a conflict whose strongest motive determines the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In brutes motives are perceptible impressions limiting their choice to present sensuous perception; in humans motives are often abstract and hidden, so the necessity of their effect is less apparent. Deliberation is a battle among motives rather than freedom from motive-determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deeds (not wishes) as the expression of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the deed, not the mere wish, is a valid indication of individual character for oneself and others; deeds, requiring deliberation and reason, mirror the inmost willing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wishes are immediate, momentary consequences of impressions and thus reflect 'man in general' rather than the individual's character. Consequently, in a healthy mind only deeds oppress the conscience; unconsidered acts in passion are intermediate between wishes and resolves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquired character: knowledge of one's limits and proper pursuits
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquired character consists in the abstract, distinct knowledge of the unalterable qualities of one's empirical character and the measure and direction of one's powers; with this knowledge one deliberately conducts the rôle proper to one's individuality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attaining acquired character requires experience to learn what one truly wills and can do. It entails renouncing incompatible pursuits, avoiding pretence, cultivating one's aptitudes, and applying fixed maxims to particular choices to avoid wavering, mortification, and wasted effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of necessity (fatalism) as consolation
rubrics_metrics.description: A distinct knowledge of inward and outward necessity reconciles one to permanent ills and reduces suffering, because recognizing that things could not have been otherwise removes fruitless complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: entrapped elephants that stop struggling once they see resistance is useless; Biblical example of King David. Recognizing necessity helps one accept defects (lameness, poverty, etc.) with indifference and contentment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Will's endless striving implies pervasive suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: The will always strives; striving is its sole nature and is not susceptible of any final, lasting satisfaction, so wherever will manifests there is continuous striving and thus suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations from nature (gravity, chemical forces, plant growth, electricity) show endless striving; because striving lacks a final end, there can be no measure and end of suffering. In the human realm this is particularly acute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental suffering predominates and can overpower physical pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental, reflective suffering (arising from abstract thought, expectation, renunciation) is often far greater than physical pain and can render one insensible to physical pain, sometimes leading to self-harm or suicide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behaviors like tearing hair, beating the breast, or inflicting physical wounds serve to divert attention from unbearable mental anguish. The development of intelligence increases susceptibility to such torment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character is empirically revealed over time; knowledge changes apparent conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the intelligible character (will-in-itself) is unalterable, the empirical character (its unfolding) and the appearance of character in actions develop over time because knowledge (motives made known) affects action; we often discover our true nature only a posteriori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains how an impetuous youth may become sober with age, and why people are 'innocent' initially (they and others don't yet know their natural dispositions). Repentance and changes of conduct are thus changes of knowledge about motives, not of the will itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human deliberation increases misery compared to brutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Because humans can form abstract conceptions and reflect on consequences, they experience greater and more protracted suffering than brutes, who live in present perception and relative carelessness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract thoughts produce painful anticipations and renunciations (e.g., foreseen privations), leading to chronic mental torment that often outweighs present physical hardships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real freedom via denial of individuation (self-renunciation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A phenomenon of human will that is impossible in brutes may occur when one lays aside knowledge of particulars (the principium individuationis) and, by insight into the Ideas, effects a suppression of the will's assertion—a form of real freedom expressed as self-renunciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This genuine expression of will's freedom (distinct from the ordinary deliberative 'choice') is rare and cannot be fully explained here; it will be treated in the concluding part of the work. It does not modify the empirical character's ordinary necessity.
